title: The path of an API request
summary: Authentication, authorization, admission webhooks and how a write actually lands in etcd.

concepts.title: From kubectl to etcd
concepts.brief:
Every request — yours, a controller's, Rancher's — walks the same pipeline:

- **Authentication**: who are you? Client cert, bearer token, ServiceAccount JWT, or an OIDC/webhook provider. Failure = `401`.
- **Authorization**: are you allowed? RBAC (and the Node authorizer for kubelets). Failure = `403`.
- **Mutating admission**: plugins and webhooks may *change* the object (inject sidecars, add defaults).
- **Schema validation**: does the object match the OpenAPI schema / CRD schema?
- **Validating admission**: plugins, webhooks and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy may *reject* it.
- **Persist**: written to etcd, revision assigned, watchers notified.

The order matters for debugging. A `401` never reached RBAC. A `403` means you authenticated fine and RBAC said no. A message from a webhook means you got all the way to admission.

examples.label: Reading the error tells you the stage
examples.code:
# 401 - authentication
error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)

# 403 - authorization (RBAC)
Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden:
  User "raz" cannot list resource "pods" in API group "" in the namespace "prod"

# admission webhook rejection
Error from server: admission webhook "validation.gatekeeper.sh" denied the request:
  container <api> has no memory limit

examples.label: Who am I, and can I do this?
examples.code:
$ kubectl auth whoami
ATTRIBUTE   VALUE
Username    system:serviceaccount:prod:deployer
Groups      [system:serviceaccounts system:authenticated]

$ kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n prod
no

$ kubectl auth can-i --list -n prod | head -5
examples.note: `auth can-i` asks the API server to run the real authorization check. It is the fastest way to settle an RBAC argument.

examples.label: See the whole pipeline with verbose output
examples.code:
$ kubectl get pods -v=8 2>&1 | grep -E 'Request Headers|GET https|Response Status'
GET https://10.0.0.10:6443/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods?limit=500
Request Headers: Authorization: Bearer <masked>
Response Status: 200 OK in 14 milliseconds

items.prompt: Order the stages a `kubectl apply` passes through in the API server.
steps: Authentication — establish the identity of the caller
Authorization — RBAC decides if that identity may perform this verb
Mutating admission — webhooks and plugins may modify the object
Schema validation against the OpenAPI/CRD schema
Validating admission — webhooks and policies may reject it
Write to etcd and notify watchers
items.explain: Mutating always runs before validating, so a sidecar injected by a mutating webhook is still subject to the policy checks that follow. If they ran the other way round, injection could bypass policy.

items.prompt: A CI pipeline gets `Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps is forbidden`. What is ruled out?
choices: Its credentials are fine — authentication succeeded, so this is an RBAC problem
Its token expired
The API server is unreachable
The namespace does not exist
items.explain: 403 comes after successful authentication. An expired or invalid token gives 401 (`Unauthorized`). So stop regenerating the token and go look at the RoleBinding — `kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer` reproduces it exactly.

items.prompt: Which `kubectl` flag lets a cluster-admin test another identity's permissions without their credentials?
items.explain: `kubectl auth can-i list pods -n prod --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:deployer`. Impersonation is itself an RBAC-controlled verb (`impersonate`), so it is auditable.

items.prompt: The error is `admission webhook "vpolicy.kyverno.svc" denied the request`. What does that prove about the request?
choices: It authenticated, passed RBAC, and reached validating admission before being rejected by policy
The user lacks RBAC permission for the resource
The object failed OpenAPI schema validation
etcd rejected the write
items.explain: Getting a named webhook rejection means you traversed everything before it. The fix is a policy exception or a corrected manifest — not RBAC, not credentials.

concepts.title: RBAC in practice
concepts.brief:
Four object types, one rule: **permissions are additive and there are no deny rules**.

- **Role** — verbs on resources, scoped to one namespace
- **ClusterRole** — the same, cluster-wide (or for cluster-scoped resources like nodes and PVs)
- **RoleBinding** — grants a Role *or a ClusterRole* to subjects, within one namespace
- **ClusterRoleBinding** — grants a ClusterRole cluster-wide

The combination people forget: a **RoleBinding referencing a ClusterRole** grants that ClusterRole's permissions *only inside the binding's namespace*. That is how you reuse the built-in `view`/`edit`/`admin` roles per namespace instead of writing them out again.

Subjects are Users, Groups and ServiceAccounts. Kubernetes has no user database — Users and Groups come from certificates or your OIDC provider, so `raz` only exists as a string in a certificate CN or a token claim.

examples.label: Namespace-scoped reuse of a ClusterRole
examples.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: team-a-edit
  namespace: team-a
subjects:
- kind: Group
  name: "oidc:team-a"          # comes from your IdP
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole             # cluster role...
  name: edit                    # ...bound only inside team-a
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
examples.note: The single most useful RBAC pattern: one ClusterRole, many namespaced RoleBindings.

examples.label: Escalation you can grant by accident
examples.code:
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
# equivalent to handing over every credential in the namespace

- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods/exec", "pods/portforward"]
  verbs: ["create"]
# shell inside any pod - including one running as a privileged service account
examples.note: `create` on `pods` in a namespace is close to namespace-admin: you can mount any secret and run as any ServiceAccount in it.

examples.label: Who can do this?
examples.code:
$ kubectl auth can-i list secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:app:default -n app
no

$ kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o custom-columns=\
NAME:.metadata.name,ROLE:.roleRef.name,SUBJECTS:.subjects[*].name | grep cluster-admin

items.prompt: A RoleBinding in namespace `team-a` references the ClusterRole `edit`. What does the subject get?
choices: The `edit` permissions, but only within namespace team-a
The `edit` permissions across the whole cluster
Nothing — a RoleBinding cannot reference a ClusterRole
Read-only access to team-a
items.explain: The *binding* type decides the scope, not the role type. This is the intended way to reuse built-in ClusterRoles per namespace. The reverse is impossible: a ClusterRoleBinding cannot be narrowed to a namespace.

items.prompt: A user has `view` in namespace `prod` via one binding and `admin` via another. You want to stop them deleting Deployments in prod. What works?
choices: Remove or narrow the binding that grants admin — RBAC has no deny rules, permissions only add up
Add a Role with `deny` on the delete verb
Add a RoleBinding with an empty verbs list to override
Set the admin binding's priority lower than view
items.explain: RBAC is purely additive: the union of every matching rule. There is no deny and no ordering. If you need real deny semantics (e.g. 'no privileged pods anywhere'), that is an admission policy job — Kyverno, Gatekeeper or ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

items.prompt: Match each object to its scope.
pairs: Verbs on resources inside one namespace
Verbs cluster-wide, or on cluster-scoped resources
Grants a Role or ClusterRole within one namespace
Grants a ClusterRole across the whole cluster
items.explain: Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses and CRDs are cluster-scoped, so access to them can only come from a ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.

items.prompt: What is the username a pod presents when it calls the API with its mounted ServiceAccount token?
choices: system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>
The pod name
system:node:<nodename>
The name of the Deployment that owns it
items.explain: And it is in the group `system:serviceaccounts:<namespace>`, which lets you bind permissions to every SA in a namespace at once. Modern tokens are short-lived projected volumes bound to the pod's lifetime, not the old never-expiring Secret.

items.prompt: Which grants are effectively namespace-admin even though they look narrow?
choices: `get`/`list` on secrets in the namespace
`create` on pods in the namespace
`create` on pods/exec
`get` on configmaps
items.explain: Reading secrets hands over credentials. Creating pods lets you mount any secret and assume any ServiceAccount in that namespace. `pods/exec` gives a shell in an existing pod with its identity. ConfigMaps are usually non-sensitive — usually.

concepts.title: Admission control
concepts.brief:
Admission plugins run **inside** the API server; admission **webhooks** are your own HTTPS services it calls out to.

A webhook is registered by a `MutatingWebhookConfiguration` or `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` that says: for these resources and verbs, POST an `AdmissionReview` to this Service and use the response.

The operationally dangerous field is `failurePolicy`:

- `Fail` (default) — if your webhook is unreachable, the matching API requests are **rejected**
- `Ignore` — requests proceed if the webhook is down

A `Fail` webhook that matches broadly, and whose own pods cannot start, is a classic self-inflicted cluster outage: nothing can be created, including the webhook's own pods. Always scope `namespaceSelector`/`objectSelector` and exclude `kube-system`.

examples.label: A webhook registration, annotated
examples.code:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: pod-policy
webhooks:
- name: policy.example.com
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    apiVersions: ["v1"]
    operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
    resources: ["pods"]
  failurePolicy: Fail            # deadlock risk if it matches everything
  namespaceSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
      operator: NotIn
      values: [kube-system, cattle-system]
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  clientConfig:
    service: { name: policy-svc, namespace: policy, path: /validate }
    caBundle: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...

examples.label: The outage it causes
examples.code:
Error creating: Internal error occurred: failed calling webhook "policy.example.com":
  failed to call webhook: Post "https://policy-svc.policy.svc:443/validate?timeout=5s":
  dial tcp 10.43.12.7:443: connect: connection refused
examples.note: Every pod creation in the cluster now fails - including the policy webhook's own replacement pods. Recovery: delete the ValidatingWebhookConfiguration, let things start, then re-apply it.

examples.label: Built-in plugins you rely on daily
examples.code:
NamespaceLifecycle     - blocks creates in a Terminating namespace
LimitRanger            - applies LimitRange defaults
ServiceAccount         - injects the SA token volume
DefaultStorageClass    - fills in a PVC's storageClassName
ResourceQuota          - enforces quota at admission time
PodSecurity            - enforces Pod Security Standards by namespace label

items.prompt: A ValidatingWebhookConfiguration with `failurePolicy: Fail` matches all pod CREATEs. Its backing Deployment is scaled to zero. What is the state of the cluster?
choices: No new pods can be created anywhere, including the webhook's own — you must delete the webhook configuration to recover
Pod creation continues; the webhook is skipped when unavailable
Only pods in the webhook's namespace are blocked
The API server disables the webhook automatically after 3 failures
items.explain: `Fail` means unreachable = denied, and there is no auto-disable. This is the textbook admission-webhook deadlock. Prevention: `namespaceSelector` excluding system namespaces, a tight `timeoutSeconds`, and at least two replicas with a PDB.

items.prompt: A service mesh injects a sidecar via a mutating webhook. A policy engine requires every container to have memory limits. Which runs first and why does it matter?
choices: Mutating runs first, so the injected sidecar is also checked by the validating policy
Validating runs first, so the sidecar escapes the policy
They run in parallel and the API server merges results
Order is random and configured per cluster
items.explain: Mutating always precedes validating. That is precisely so injected containers cannot slip past policy — and it is also why your mesh sidecar needs limits set in the injector template, or every pod gets rejected.

items.prompt: Which of these are handled by built-in admission plugins rather than by controllers after the fact?
choices: Rejecting a pod that would exceed a ResourceQuota
Filling in a PVC's storageClassName from the default StorageClass
Applying LimitRange defaults to a container with no requests
Creating a ReplicaSet for a new Deployment
items.explain: Quota, default StorageClass and LimitRange defaults are all applied at admission — before the object is stored. Creating a ReplicaSet is the deployment *controller* reacting afterwards. This distinction explains why a quota violation gives you an instant error while a bad Deployment gives you a healthy object with sad status.

items.prompt: Cluster-wide pod creation is blocked by a broken `Fail` webhook. Which object type do you delete to break the deadlock?
items.explain: Deleting the ValidatingWebhookConfiguration (or MutatingWebhookConfiguration) unregisters the callout immediately — the API server stops calling it. Save a copy first, bring the webhook's pods back, then re-apply.

concepts.title: resourceVersion, watches and informers
concepts.brief:
Every object carries a `metadata.resourceVersion` — really etcd's global revision at the time it was written. Two mechanisms hang off it.

**Optimistic concurrency.** An update sends the resourceVersion it read. If someone else wrote in between, the API server returns `409 Conflict`. This is why controllers retry on conflict instead of locking. It is also why `kubectl apply` on an object being actively modified sometimes needs a second go.

**Watches and informers.** A client LISTs (getting a resourceVersion) and then WATCHes from that revision, receiving only deltas. An **informer** wraps this in a local cache plus a work queue: controllers read from the cache instead of hammering the API server, and process changes one at a time.

When a watch falls too far behind, etcd may have compacted the old revision — the client gets `410 Gone` and must relist. Perfectly normal; a storm of relists is not.

examples.label: Optimistic concurrency in the raw
examples.code:
$ kubectl get deploy api -o jsonpath='{.metadata.resourceVersion}'
84102391

# someone else updates it...
$ kubectl replace -f old-api.yaml
Error from server (Conflict): Operation cannot be fulfilled on deployments.apps "api":
  the object has been modified; please apply your changes to the latest version and try again
examples.note: `kubectl apply` mostly avoids this by patching. `kubectl replace` sends the whole object with the version you read.

examples.label: Why controllers use informers
examples.code:
without informer:  every controller polls the API server -> N controllers x M objects of load
with informer:     one watch per resource type per controller
                   -> local cache (Store) kept up to date by deltas
                   -> handlers push keys into a rate-limited work queue
                   -> worker pops key, reads from CACHE, reconciles, requeues on error
examples.note: Reconciling from cache is why controllers are level-triggered: the worker looks at the *current* object, not the event that woke it.

examples.label: 410 Gone is normal
examples.code:
W  reflector.go:462] k8s.io/client-go/informers: watch of *v1.Pod ended with:
   too old resource version: 84009122 (84102391)
I  reflector.go:281] Listing and watching *v1.Pod from k8s.io/client-go/informers
examples.note: The client relists and carries on. Constant relisting usually means etcd compaction is aggressive or the client is too slow to keep up.

items.prompt: Your operator gets `409 Conflict` when updating a CR it just read. What is the correct behavior?
choices: Re-read the object and retry the update against the new resourceVersion
Force the write with --overwrite to win the race
Take a distributed lock before every update
Delete and recreate the object
items.explain: 409 is the system working. Kubernetes has no locks; it uses optimistic concurrency and expects clients to retry. `RetryOnConflict` in client-go exists exactly for this loop.

items.prompt: Why does a controller reconcile from its informer cache instead of the event payload that woke it?
choices: So it always acts on current state — missed or coalesced events cannot cause permanent drift
Because events do not contain the object
To avoid RBAC checks on each read
Because the cache is stored in etcd
items.explain: Level-triggered, not edge-triggered. Events are only a hint that *something* changed; the controller then looks at reality. This is why a controller can be restarted, miss a week of events, and still converge on its first resync.

items.prompt: Order what an informer does on startup.
steps: LIST all objects of the type, noting the returned resourceVersion
Populate the local cache with the full result
Open a WATCH starting from that resourceVersion
Apply add/update/delete deltas to the cache and queue keys for workers
items.explain: List-then-watch is the fundamental pattern of every Kubernetes client. The resourceVersion stitches the two together with no gap and no duplicates.

choices: An opaque token backed by etcd's global revision — comparable only for equality, not arithmetic
A monotonically increasing per-object counter starting at 1
A hash of the object's spec
The number of times the object has been updated
items.explain: It is global to the cluster, not per-object, so two objects' resourceVersions are not meaningfully comparable and you must never do maths on them. Treat it as an opaque cursor.
